stimulus.text: “We in America today are nearer to the final triumph over poverty than ever before in the history of any land. The poorhouse is vanishing from among us. We have not yet reached the goal, but, given a chance to go forward with the policies of the last 8 years, we shall soon with the help of God be in sight of the day when poverty will be banished from this Nation.” — Herbert Hoover, speech accepting the Republican presidential nomination, August 11, 1928. Abridged.

rationales.A: Smith carrying the big cities while Hoover swept the countryside shows the divide alive, not faded. A faded divide would split both places evenly.
rationales.B: Hoover swept the countryside and won the election in a landslide. Rural voters backed Hoover, not Smith.
rationales.C: Smith was wet and Hoover was dry, and the issue split the vote. Prohibition was still dividing voters in 1928.
rationales.D: Background from the books: Smith carried the twelve largest cities while Hoover won the countryside and the election. The same city-country split that shaped the decade's culture wars showed up in the vote itself.
rationales.general:
1. Put the two facts side by side: Hoover won in a landslide, and Smith carried the twelve largest cities.
2. Ask what each fact shows: Hoover's strength was rural, Smith's was urban.
3. Ask what the split means: the two Americas voted differently.
4. Name the pattern: the cultural split between city and countryside persisted.
Remember: when one candidate sweeps the countryside and the other sweeps the cities, the map is the argument.
